question: What is the difference between lazy and eager loading in JPA?
title: Lazy vs Eager Loading in JPA — FetchType Explained
direct_answer: **Lazy loading** delays fetching related entities until you actually access them; **eager loading** fetches them immediately alongside the parent. In JPA, **@OneToMany** and **@ManyToMany** default to **LAZY**, while **@ManyToOne** and **@OneToOne** default to **EAGER**.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand JPA fetch strategies, their defaults per association, and their performance implications
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Switching everything to EAGER to avoid LazyInitializationException — a wrong fix that always loads too much data
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention the N+1 problem and how JOIN FETCH or @EntityGraph solves it while keeping LAZY as the default for fine-grained control

sections.title: Lazy vs Eager: Controlling When Related Data Loads
sections.content:
When an **Order** entity holds a list of **OrderItems**, JPA must decide: fetch the items immediately, or wait until you use them? **Eager loading** runs a JOIN right away and fills the collection in one round trip. **Lazy loading** leaves the collection as a proxy until you call `order.getItems()` — only then does Hibernate fire a SELECT.

The default depends on the association type: **@OneToMany** and **@ManyToMany** are LAZY because they can hold many rows and would bloat memory; **@ManyToOne** and **@OneToOne** are EAGER because it's usually just one extra row. The choice affects both query count and memory use.

sections.title: Lazy vs Eager Loading
sections.content:
| Aspect | Lazy Loading | Eager Loading |
|---|---|---|
| When data loads | On first access in code | Immediately with the parent |
| SQL queries | Separate SELECT when accessed | JOIN in the initial query |
| Default for @OneToMany | Yes (LAZY) | No |
| Default for @ManyToOne | No | Yes (EAGER) |
| Risk | LazyInitializationException if session closed | Loads unused data, hurts performance |

sections.title: Fetch Defaults at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|LAZY|~Load on access|@OneToMany, @ManyToMany|proxy until getItems()|saves memory by default
blue|EAGER|~Load immediately|@ManyToOne, @OneToOne|JOIN with the parent|one extra row, usually fine
emerald|Lazy risk|~Session closed|LazyInitializationException|access outside transaction|keep tx open or fetch
rose|Eager risk|~Over-fetch|loads unused data|N+1 on lists|never EAGER on collections

sections.title: Lazy vs Eager in Action
When to Use Each Strategy
sections.content:
Default to **lazy loading** for collections (@OneToMany, @ManyToMany) — you rarely need all related data on every parent load. Loading a Customer shouldn't drag in 500 orders unless you're building an order-history page.

Use **eager loading** for @ManyToOne associations you always need, like an Order that always shows the Customer name. But don't set `fetch = EAGER` globally on entities. Instead, use **@EntityGraph** or **JOIN FETCH** in the specific queries that need the data: lazy by default, eager only where needed.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Setting everything to EAGER** — one LazyInitializationException, and the panic fix is global `FetchType.EAGER`, which degrades every query by always loading unused data through expensive JOINs.
- **Not knowing the defaults** — forgetting that @ManyToOne is EAGER causes surprise N+1 when you loop over Orders and each loads its Customer separately.
- **Ignoring transaction boundaries** — accessing lazy collections outside `@Transactional` throws LazyInitializationException, then it's 'fixed' wrong with Open Session In View instead of proper transaction scoping.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Lazy loading** delays fetching until access, cutting memory and initial query cost.
- **Eager loading** fetches related entities immediately via a JOIN with the parent.
- **Defaults**: @OneToMany and @ManyToMany are LAZY; @ManyToOne and @OneToOne are EAGER.
- **LazyInitializationException** fires when you access lazy data after the transaction closes.
- **@EntityGraph / JOIN FETCH** load lazy data per query without changing entity defaults.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Lazy loading means JPA waits to fetch related entities until you actually access them in your code. Eager loading fetches them immediately, in the same query as the parent. So if I load an Order with lazy items, Hibernate doesn't load the order items until I call get items in my code. With eager, it does a JOIN right away and loads everything together.

The defaults matter. The OneToMany and ManyToMany associations are lazy by default, because collections can be huge. The ManyToOne and OneToOne associations are eager by default, because it's usually just one extra row.

Here's the trade-off. Lazy saves memory and query time when you don't need the data, but it can cause the N plus one problem if you access lazy collections in a loop — one query for the list, then one query per item. Eager avoids that but wastes resources when you don't use the data.

A common mistake freshers make is switching everything to eager when they hit a LazyInitializationException. That's the wrong fix. The right approach is to keep lazy as the default and use JOIN FETCH or EntityGraph in the specific queries where you know you need the related data. That gives you fine-grained control: lazy by default, eager only where it makes sense.

question: What is the N+1 problem in JPA and how do you fix it?
title: N+1 Problem in JPA — Cause and Fix with JOIN FETCH
direct_answer: The **N+1 problem** happens when you load N parents and then access a **lazy association** on each in a loop: **1 query for the parents plus N for the children**. Fix it with **JOIN FETCH** in JPQL, **@EntityGraph** on repository methods, or **@BatchSize** to batch the N queries.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can identify, explain, and fix the most commonly asked JPA performance bug
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Fixing N+1 by switching the association to EAGER globally — it just trades one performance problem for another
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show a concrete JOIN FETCH solution and mention @BatchSize as an alternative when JOIN FETCH isn't possible (e.g. pagination)

sections.title: The N+1 Query Problem Explained
sections.content:
The **N+1 problem** is one of the most common performance killers in JPA. It happens when you fetch N entities and then access a **lazy association** on each inside a loop. JPA runs 1 query for the N parents, then N more — one per parent — for the children. Load 100 Orders and loop accessing `order.getCustomer()`, and you get 101 queries: 1 for orders, 100 for customers.

It's catastrophic because each query carries network latency and database overhead — a 50ms page balloons to 5 seconds. Worse, it's **silent**: the code runs without errors, but response time explodes. The root cause is lazy loading firing separate SELECTs in a loop. The fix is to **fetch the related data upfront** with a JOIN, turning 1+N into 1.

sections.title: N+1 Fixes at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|JOIN FETCH|~JPQL JOIN|loads parent + children|one query|explicit, you write it
blue|@EntityGraph|~Spring Data|attributePaths|auto-generated JOIN|no JPQL needed
emerald|@BatchSize|~Batch the N|SQL IN clauses|works with pagination|fewer round trips
violet|Detect it|~show-sql|see every query|spot the flood|profile before prod

sections.title: Without — Lazy Access in a Loop Fires N+1
With — JOIN FETCH or @EntityGraph Collapse It to One Query
When and How to Fix N+1
sections.content: Fix N+1 whenever you load a collection of entities and know you'll access an association on each. Use **JOIN FETCH** in custom JPQL when you want explicit control. Use **@EntityGraph** on Spring Data methods when you'd rather not write JPQL. Use **@BatchSize** when JOIN isn't ideal — for example, with pagination or multiple collections — so `@BatchSize(size=10)` turns 100 queries into 10 `IN`-clause batches. Always verify with `spring.jpa.show-sql=true`.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Switching to FetchType.EAGER globally** — fixes this case but loads the association on every query, with no per-query opt-out.
- **Not enabling query logging** — you can't see N+1 without SQL logs; turn on `spring.jpa.show-sql=true` and `hibernate.format_sql=true`.
- **JOIN FETCH with pagination** — combining JOIN FETCH and `Pageable` makes Hibernate load all rows and paginate in memory; use @EntityGraph or @BatchSize for paginated queries with associations.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **N+1** = 1 query for N parents plus N queries for children accessed lazily in a loop.
- **Performance hit** turns one fast query into hundreds, especially inside loops.
- **JOIN FETCH** loads associations in the initial query via a SQL JOIN.
- **@EntityGraph** auto-generates that JOIN for declared attribute paths.
- **@BatchSize** batches the N queries using SQL `IN` clauses — works with pagination.
- **Wrong fix**: global `FetchType.EAGER` over-fetches everywhere else.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
The N plus one problem is when you load a list of entities and then access a lazy association on each one in a loop. You end up with one query to load the list, plus one query per item to load the related data. So if you load fifty orders and then call get customer on each order, you get fifty-one database queries. That's terrible for performance, because each query carries network and database overhead, and it happens because the association is lazy, so Hibernate doesn't load it until you touch it.

The fix is to load the related data upfront in the initial query using a JOIN. You can do that with JOIN FETCH in JPQL — for example, SELECT o FROM Order o JOIN FETCH o dot customer loads both orders and customers in one query. Or you use the EntityGraph annotation on your Spring Data repository method, and Spring generates the JOIN automatically. A third option is the BatchSize annotation, which batches the N queries into a few queries using IN clauses, and that one even works with pagination.

The common mistake is switching the association to eager on the entity. That fixes this specific case but causes problems everywhere else, because now every query loads the customer even when you don't need it. The right approach is to keep lazy as the default and reach for JOIN FETCH or EntityGraph in just the queries where you know you'll need the data.

question: What is LazyInitializationException and how do you fix it?
title: LazyInitializationException in JPA — Cause and Solutions
direct_answer: **LazyInitializationException** is thrown when you access a **lazy association** after the JPA session/transaction has closed — the persistence context is gone, so Hibernate can't run the SELECT. Fix it by widening the **@Transactional** scope, or loading the data upfront with **JOIN FETCH** or **@EntityGraph**.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand the persistence-context lifecycle and can name the right fix versus the band-aid fixes
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Enabling hibernate.enable_lazy_load_no_trans=true — a band-aid that hides bugs and causes silent N+1
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Distinguish the correct fix (keep the transaction open or use JOIN FETCH) from wrong fixes (Open Session In View, enable_lazy_load_no_trans)

sections.title: Understanding LazyInitializationException
sections.content:
**LazyInitializationException** is Hibernate saying: I can't load this lazy data because the session is already closed. It occurs when you access a lazy association (like a default @OneToMany) outside the **transaction boundary**.

Here's the sequence: your service loads an Order inside a `@Transactional` method. When the method returns, Spring closes the transaction and Hibernate closes the **persistence context**. Your controller then calls `order.getItems()`, Hibernate needs a SELECT, but the session is gone — so it throws. Think of the persistence context like a library card: you can borrow data only while it's active. This isn't a logic bug; it's a mismatch between your transaction boundaries and your data-access pattern.

sections.title: Cause and Fixes at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Cause|~Session closed|lazy access after commit|persistence context gone|no connection to query
blue|@Transactional fix|~Widen the scope|access inside the tx|cleanest architecture|keep session open
emerald|JOIN FETCH / @EntityGraph|~Load upfront|fetch in the query|no lazy access needed|per-query control
rose|Band-aid fixes|~Avoid these|enable_lazy_load_no_trans|Open Session In View|hide bugs, cause N+1

sections.title: LazyInitializationException Example and Fixes
When and How to Fix It
sections.content: Pick one of three fixes by use case. Use **@Transactional on service methods** when you control the service layer — keep boundaries wide enough to cover all data access; this is the cleanest fix. Use **@EntityGraph or JOIN FETCH** when you know upfront which associations you need, loading them in one query. Use **DTO projections** when your API needs only a subset of fields, loading exactly those in one query. Avoid `enable_lazy_load_no_trans`, which opens a fresh session per lazy access and causes silent N+1 plus connection exhaustion.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Enabling enable_lazy_load_no_trans** — it stops the exception by opening a new session on each lazy access, trading one bug for severe N+1 and pool exhaustion.
- **Relying on Open Session In View** — `spring.jpa.open-in-view=true` (Spring Boot's default) keeps the session open for the whole request, hiding the exception but encouraging data access in controllers and N+1 in views. Disable it in production.
- **Switching everything to EAGER** — avoids the exception but loads unneeded data on other queries; keep lazy and fix the transaction boundary instead.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **LazyInitializationException** fires when you access lazy data after the session/transaction closes.
- The **persistence context** is the session that tracks entities and enables lazy loading; it closes when `@Transactional` ends.
- **Correct fix** — access the data inside a `@Transactional` method, or fetch it with `@EntityGraph`/JOIN FETCH.
- **Wrong fix** — `enable_lazy_load_no_trans` opens new sessions silently, causing N+1 and pool issues.
- **DTO projections** load only the needed fields in one query, avoiding lazy access entirely.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
LazyInitializationException happens when you try to access a lazy-loaded association after the Hibernate session has closed. So say I load an Order in a repository method, that method returns, and Spring closes the transaction. The persistence context is gone. Then I try to call get items on the order in my controller. Hibernate needs to run a SELECT to load the items, but the session is closed, so it throws the exception. The root cause is a mismatch between where I'm accessing the data and where my transaction boundaries are.

The right fix depends on the situation. If I control the service layer, I move the data access into a Transactional method so the session stays open while I'm using the entity — that's the cleanest architectural fix. Or I use EntityGraph or JOIN FETCH in the repository to load the data eagerly in the same query, avoiding lazy loading altogether.

A common mistake freshers make is enabling the enable lazy load no trans Hibernate property. It looks like a fix because it stops the exception, but what it really does is open a new session every time you touch lazy data, which causes silent N plus one problems and burns through your connection pool. Another wrong fix is Open Session In View, which keeps the session open for the whole HTTP request. Spring Boot has that on by default, but you should disable it in production, because it pushes data access logic into controllers instead of services.

question: What is @EntityGraph in Spring Data JPA?
title: @EntityGraph in Spring Data JPA — Declarative Eager Loading Per Query
direct_answer: **@EntityGraph** is a Spring Data JPA annotation on repository methods that tells Hibernate to **eagerly fetch specified associations for that query only** — without changing the entity's default fetch type. It generates a JOIN so the related data loads in a single query, fixing N+1 per query.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know per-query eager loading is the clean fix for N+1, without polluting entity metadata
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing @EntityGraph exists and switching FetchType to EAGER globally on the entity class
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that @EntityGraph fixes N+1 for specific queries without touching the entity's global fetch strategy — the best of both worlds

sections.title: Per-Query Eager Loading with @EntityGraph
sections.content:
**@EntityGraph** gives you **per-query control** over which associations load eagerly, without changing the entity's default fetch type. You put it on a repository method and list the relationships to fetch via **attributePaths**. When that method runs, Hibernate generates a JOIN to load those associations in one query — solving **N+1** for that query without affecting others.

Think of it as a query-level override: the entity says `items` is lazy, but this particular `findAll` says fetch `items` eagerly just here. The win is **separation of concerns** — entity metadata stays focused on mapping, while repository methods declare their data needs. It's the right way to handle N+1: lazy by default, @EntityGraph where you need eager.

sections.title: @EntityGraph at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Where it goes|~Repository method|annotates a query|not the entity|per-query scope
blue|attributePaths|~What to fetch|field names to load|nested with dots|items, items.product
emerald|What it does|~Generates a JOIN|loads in one query|fixes N+1 here|other queries unaffected
violet|vs global EAGER|~Clean alternative|entity stays lazy|no metadata pollution|fetch only where needed

sections.title: @EntityGraph in Action
When to Use @EntityGraph
sections.content: Use **@EntityGraph** when a specific repository method always needs certain associations — e.g. an order-history page that always shows items uses `@EntityGraph(attributePaths="items")` on `findByCustomerId`. Use **nested paths** like `{"items", "items.product"}` to load multiple levels in one query. Prefer it over JOIN FETCH when you're using derived query methods or don't want to write JPQL. Don't slap it on every method — only where you'll actually access the associations, keeping other queries lean.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Not knowing it exists** — hitting N+1 and switching the entity to `FetchType.EAGER`, polluting metadata and hurting performance elsewhere.
- **Wrong attributePaths** — a typo like `"item"` when the field is `items` fails or throws at runtime; rely on IDE autocomplete.
- **Overusing it** — putting @EntityGraph on `findAll`, `findById`, and every custom method effectively makes the association EAGER globally; apply it only where needed.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **@EntityGraph** enables per-query eager loading without changing the entity's default fetch type.
- **attributePaths** lists entity field names to fetch eagerly for that method.
- **Nested paths** (dot notation) load multiple association levels in one query.
- It **solves N+1** by generating a JOIN instead of N separate queries.
- It **only affects the annotated method** — other queries keep the lazy default.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
EntityGraph is a Spring Data JPA annotation you put on repository methods to tell Hibernate which associations to fetch eagerly for that specific query. You list the field names in attribute paths, and Spring generates a JOIN in the SQL to load everything in one query.

For example, if I have an Order entity with a lazy items collection, I can put EntityGraph with attribute paths equals items on my find all method. Now when I call find all, Hibernate runs a query with a JOIN to load both orders and items together. The big advantage is that it only affects that one method. Other repository methods without the annotation still use the entity's default lazy behaviour. So I get the best of both worlds: lazy by default for performance, eager where I need it to avoid N plus one.

This is the clean solution to the N plus one problem, because I don't have to pollute my entity class with eager fetch, which would make every query load the association even when I don't need it. EntityGraph gives me per-query control, and I can even use nested paths like items dot product to load multiple levels in one query.

A common mistake freshers make is not knowing EntityGraph exists, so they switch the entity to eager globally. That fixes the immediate N plus one but kills performance on other queries. The right approach is keeping lazy as default and using EntityGraph on the specific repository methods where you know you'll access the associations.

question: What is JOIN FETCH in JPQL and how does it fix N+1?
title: JOIN FETCH in JPQL — Single Query Eager Loading for N+1 Fix
direct_answer: **JOIN FETCH** in JPQL includes an association in the SQL JOIN **and** populates it in the object graph. Unlike a plain JOIN (which only filters), JOIN FETCH actually loads the related entities. It fixes **N+1** by loading parent and children in a single query instead of 1 + N.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can write optimized JPQL and understand the semantic difference between JOIN and JOIN FETCH
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using JOIN without FETCH — it filters the query but doesn't populate the association, so lazy loading and N+1 persist
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain JOIN (filter only) versus JOIN FETCH (filter plus populate) and mention the Cartesian-product risk with multiple collections

sections.title: JOIN FETCH: The N+1 Problem Solver
sections.content:
**JOIN FETCH** is a JPQL keyword that eagerly loads an association within a single SQL query. The key insight: a plain **JOIN** in JPQL is for filtering (WHERE conditions) and does **not** populate related entities. **JOIN FETCH** does both — it JOINs the tables AND loads the related objects into memory.

This eliminates the **N+1 problem**, where you run 1 query for parents then N more for children. With JOIN FETCH you get exactly 1 round trip. The trade-off is loading more data upfront, so use it only when you know you'll need that association.

sections.title: JOIN vs JOIN FETCH
sections.content:
| Aspect | Plain JOIN | JOIN FETCH |
|---|---|---|
| Affects WHERE filtering | Yes | Yes |
| Populates the association | No | Yes |
| Association still lazy | Yes — N+1 on access | No — already loaded |
| Queries for the children | N (one per parent) | 0 (loaded in the JOIN) |
| Typical use | Filter parents by child fields | Load parents with their children |

sections.title: JOIN FETCH Essentials at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Loads + filters|~Not just a filter|populates the graph|parent + children|one query total
blue|DISTINCT|~Dedup parents|JOIN multiplies rows|SELECT DISTINCT|removes duplicate parents
emerald|One collection|~Safe to fetch|single JOIN FETCH|no Cartesian blow-up|per-query eager
rose|Multiple collections|~Cartesian risk|rows multiply|MultipleBagFetchException|use @EntityGraph or batches

sections.title: Without — Plain Query Leaves Items Lazy (N+1)
With — JOIN FETCH Loads Orders and Items in One Query
When to Use JOIN FETCH
sections.content: Use **JOIN FETCH** when you'll need the association immediately after loading the parent: orders with line items for an order summary, users with profiles for a list API, posts with their author for a feed. Don't use it for large collections you might not iterate, or when you usually need only the parent. The goal is to remove the lazy-load queries you know will happen, without over-fetching.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **JOIN without FETCH** — `SELECT o FROM Order o JOIN o.items` only filters; items stay lazy and N+1 returns on access.
- **Fetching multiple collections** — `JOIN FETCH o.items JOIN FETCH o.payments` makes a Cartesian product (3 items × 2 payments = 6 rows) and can throw `MultipleBagFetchException`; use separate queries or @EntityGraph.
- **Always using FETCH** — adding it to every query transfers extra data and memory you don't need.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **JOIN vs JOIN FETCH** — JOIN filters; JOIN FETCH filters and loads the association into memory.
- It **eliminates N+1** by collapsing 1 + N queries into a single SQL JOIN.
- It's **eager per query** — the entity mapping stays lazy.
- Hibernate emits a **LEFT OUTER JOIN** by default, or INNER with `INNER JOIN FETCH`.
- **DISTINCT** removes duplicate parents; fetching multiple collections risks a Cartesian product.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
JOIN FETCH is a JPQL keyword that tells Hibernate to load an association in the same query as the parent entity. So if I'm loading orders and I know I'll need the line items right away, I'd write SELECT o FROM Order o JOIN FETCH o dot items. That generates a single SQL query with a JOIN that brings back both orders and items together.

The key difference from a regular JOIN is that a regular JOIN only affects the WHERE clause filtering — it doesn't actually populate the items collection, so you'd still get lazy loading and N plus one queries when you access the items. JOIN FETCH does both: it filters and it loads.

This solves the N plus one problem by doing the work upfront. Instead of one query for orders and then one query per order to get its items, you get exactly one query total. I'd use it when I'm certain I need the association, like an order summary page where items are always shown. The trade-off is loading more data, so I wouldn't use it when I only sometimes need the association.

One thing to watch is fetching two collections at once, which creates a Cartesian product and can throw a multiple bag fetch exception — there you'd use separate queries or an entity graph. And when you JOIN FETCH a collection, you usually add SELECT DISTINCT to remove duplicate parent rows. In a Spring Data repository I'd put the JOIN FETCH in a custom query with the Query annotation, and the entity mapping can stay lazy, because JOIN FETCH only affects that one query.

question: What is the best practice for fetch strategy in JPA?
title: JPA Fetch Strategy Best Practices — Lazy by Default, Eager Per Query
direct_answer: Best practice: keep all associations **LAZY by default** and load what you need **eagerly per query** with **JOIN FETCH** or **@EntityGraph**. **Never use global EAGER on collections** — it always loads data you may not need and triggers cascading queries.

sections.title: The Lazy by Default, Eager per Query Strategy
sections.content:
The golden rule for JPA fetch strategies: **start with LAZY everywhere**, then optimize the specific queries that need associations using **JOIN FETCH** or **@EntityGraph**. Each use case loads exactly what it needs.

The anti-pattern is setting `@OneToMany(fetch = EAGER)` globally after one **LazyInitializationException** — like leaving every light on because you needed one once. EAGER on collections loads all children every time you load the parent, even unused ones. In a real app this cascades: User loads Roles, Roles load Permissions, and one `findById` fires 15 queries. Keep mappings lazy and load eagerly only for the query that needs it — your entity describes the data model, not a fetching policy for every use case.

sections.title: Fetch Strategy Principles at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Lazy by default|~Baseline|all collections LAZY|optional @ManyToOne too|load nothing extra
blue|Eager per query|~Targeted|JOIN FETCH for one entity|@EntityGraph for lists|opt in where needed
emerald|Never global EAGER|~Anti-pattern|cascading queries|always over-fetches|local hammer, global pain
violet|Measure|~Evidence-based|show-sql logging|count the queries|optimize what's real

sections.title: Lazy Default with Per-Query Eager Loading
When to Apply This Strategy
sections.content: Make **LAZY** the baseline for all @OneToMany and @ManyToMany — and even @ManyToOne when the related entity is large or rarely needed. Then add targeted methods: **JOIN FETCH** for a single entity with its association (a detail page), **@EntityGraph** for multiple entities with associations (a filtered list). A user profile loading User with Roles uses JOIN FETCH; a dashboard of 20 orders with items uses @EntityGraph. Rule: if a screen always needs an association, make that query eager; if it's only sometimes needed, keep it lazy.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Switching to EAGER globally** — the biggest mistake after a LazyInitializationException; it fixes one case but over-fetches everywhere through a global hammer for a local problem.
- **Ignoring the root cause** — the exception means you accessed lazy data outside a transaction; fix the boundary or JOIN FETCH, don't go EAGER.
- **Over-fetching with @EntityGraph** — adding it everywhere wastes resources on methods that usually need only the parent; profile and optimize where it matters.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **LAZY everywhere** by default — eager loading should be a conscious per-query decision.
- **Eager per query** via JOIN FETCH or @EntityGraph, only where that use case needs it.
- **Never EAGER on collections** — it always loads all children and triggers cascading queries.
- **LazyInitializationException** — fix the transaction boundary or fetch per query, not global EAGER.
- **Measure with SQL logging** — optimize on real query counts, not assumptions.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
The best practice is to keep all associations lazy by default and load them eagerly per query when you need them. So in my entity mappings I'd use fetch equals lazy on all OneToMany and ManyToMany relationships. That way, loading a parent entity doesn't automatically trigger queries for its children. Then, for the specific use cases where I know I need the association, I'd use JOIN FETCH in a custom query or add the EntityGraph annotation to the repository method.

For example, if I've got a Customer entity with a list of orders, the orders collection is lazy. When I'm just listing customer names, I don't need orders, so that query stays fast. But when I'm showing a customer detail page with their order history, I write a query that uses JOIN FETCH to load the customer and orders together in one shot.

The big mistake freshers make is switching associations to eager globally when they hit a LazyInitializationException. That fixes one case but kills performance everywhere else, because now every query loads data you might not use. The right fix is to load the association inside the transaction with JOIN FETCH, or widen the transaction scope.

The principle is simple: your entity mapping describes the structure, but your queries decide what to load. You'd never want eager fetching on collections globally, because it causes cascading queries and can flood the database with unnecessary JOINs.
